text:
<meta>continues from previous page: by applying greasy wool.</meta> Olympias of Thebes <note>a famous ancient Greek midwife and medical writer cited by Pliny</note> added hyssop and nitre. The ash of a stag's horn is taken in a drink. It is likewise used for an aching womb. It is also applied as a liniment; and bull's bile with opium, in the weight of two obols <note>an ancient unit of weight</note>, is applied. It is also beneficial to fumigate the womb with stag's hair. They say that female deer, when they sense they are pregnant, swallow a small stone, which, if found in their excrement or in the womb (for it is found there too), preserves the fetus when tied to the body as an amulet. Small bones are also found in the heart and womb that are very useful for pregnant women and those in labor. As for the <term>pumice</term> <gloss>a stone-like growth</gloss> found in the uterus of cows in a similar way, we spoke of it in the nature of cattle. Wolf fat applied as an ointment softens the womb. It is effective even against pains of the same, when applied against harmful influences. And it is helpful. Or if a woman about to give birth is near one who has eaten [wolf's flesh], it is so effective that it works even against harmful things applied. And indeed to come upon it is destructive.

There is also great use for the hare for women. A dried lung taken in drink aids the womb. Its liver with Samian earth <note>a medicinal clay from the island of Samos</note> taken in water stops discharges. Rennet <note>original: "coagulum"</note> helps with the afterbirth. They should avoid bathing the day before. Applied as a liniment with saffron and leek juice on a fleece, it expels a dead fetus. If the wombs of hares are eaten as food, it is thought that male children are conceived. This is also achieved with their testicles and rennet. A fetus taken from a hare's womb is said to bring back fertility to those who have stopped bearing children. But even for conception, hare's blood is healthy, and the Magi give it to the husband to drink. Likewise, nine grains of its dung given to a virgin make the breasts stay firm forever. Also with rennet. For this reason, it is smeared with honey and blood where they do not want plucked hairs to grow back. For swelling of the womb, applying the dung of a wild boar or a sow with oil is beneficial. More effectively, it stops discharge if the powder of dried dung is sprinkled in a drink, as when a pregnant woman or a woman who has recently given birth suffers from griping pains. Sows' milk drunk with honeyed wine aids the delivery of women. Drunk by itself, it replenishes the failing breasts of women after childbirth. If the breasts of a young girl are smeared with the blood of a sow, they grow less. If they ache, they are soothed by drinking donkey's milk. Taken with added honey, it also aids their purgations. It heals ulcerations of the womb, as does the old fat of the same animal; and applied in a fleece, it softens the hardness of the womb. By itself, fresh or old, applied with water, it has the power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>hair-remover</gloss>. The spleen of the same animal, dried and applied with water, causes an abundance of milk in the breasts. It fixes the position of the womb <note>original: "vultus," likely a scribal error for "vulvas"</note>. 

Fumigations with a donkey's hoof hasten birth, even to the point of inducing an abortion; it should not be used otherwise, for it kills a living fetus. The dung of the same animal, if applied fresh, is said to wonderfully settle flows of blood. Also the ash of the same dung, which is also beneficial to the womb when applied. If a horse's foam is smeared on for forty days before the first hairs grow, they are suppressed. Likewise with a stag's horn, boiled. It is better if the horns are fresh. The womb is aided by being washed with mare's milk. But if a dead fetus is suspected, the spleen [of a horse] drunk in sweet water expels it. Likewise, a fumigation of the hoof or dried dung. For a prolapsed womb <note>original: "vultus," likely "vulvas"</note>, butter poured in stops it. A hardened womb is opened by ox bile mixed with rose oil, with a fleece applied externally with turpentine resin. They say that a fumigation with the dung of a male ox represses a prolapsed womb and aids birth. Conception is aided by drinking cow's milk. It is certain that infertility can occur due to troubles with childbirth. Olympias of Thebes affirms that this can be corrected with bull's bile and the fat of serpents and verdigris <note>erugo</note>, with honey added, applied to the affected areas before intercourse. Calf's bile also, if used during purgations and sprinkled on the womb during intercourse, softens the hardness of the belly; it also reduces a flow of blood when the navel is pricked, and is generally beneficial to the womb. They set the measure of the bile at the weight of a denarius to a third of a denarius of celery <note>apium</note>, mixed with as much almond oil as seems sufficient; this they apply in a fleece. The bile of a male calf, ground with half as much honey, is preserved for the womb. If they eat calf's meat roasted with <term>aristolochia</term> <gloss>birthwort, a plant used to aid labor</gloss> around the time of conception, it is promised they will give birth to males. Calf's marrow, boiled in wine and water with tallow, is beneficial for ulcerations of the womb. Likewise fox fat, and the excrement of cats with resin and rose oil applied. 

They consider it most useful to fumigate the womb with a goat's horn. The blood of wild goats with a sea-palm <note>possibly a type of seaweed or coral</note> removes hairs. The bile of other goats, when sprinkled, softens the callus of the womb and causes conception after purgation. Thus also the power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>hair-remover</gloss> is achieved if applied for three days after the hairs are plucked. Midwives promise that even an immense flow of blood is stopped by drinking goat's urine, and if the dung is applied. The membrane of a goat, dried in water after birth and taken as a drink in wine, expels the afterbirth. They think it useful to fumigate the womb with the hair of kids. And in a flow of blood, it is recommended to drink rennet or apply it with henbane seed. From a black wild ox, if the loins of a goat are pricked with its blood, Aeschines <note>the Greek orator and writer</note> says that a woman will feel a loathing for Venus <note>sexual desire</note>. He also says that drinking a goat's urine mixed with nard near the height [of desire] acts as a love potion. 

For infants, nothing is more useful than butter, by itself or with honey; especially for teething, for the gums, and for ulcers of the mouth. A wolf's tooth tied on as an amulet prevents the fears of infants and the diseases of teething. A wolf's skin provides the same. Their largest teeth, if tied to horses, are said to provide an untiring gallop. An infant's bowels are stayed by hare's rennet applied to the breast. Donkey's liver mixed with a little <term>panax</term> <gloss>all-heal herb</gloss> and dropped into the mouth protects infants from the <term>falling sickness</term> <gloss>epilepsy</gloss> and other diseases. They prescribe this for forty days. A donkey's skin thrown over them makes infants fearless. The teeth that horses first shed, when tied on as amulets, provide easy teething for infants. It is more effective if they have not touched the ground. A calf's spleen should be eaten in honey. And it should be applied for pain of the spleen. For running ulcers, use it with honey. A calf's spleen boiled in wine, ground, and applied [heals] sores of the mouth. The Magi say the brain of a goat, passed through a gold ring before milk is given to infants and dropped in, works against the falling sickness and other diseases of infants. Goat's dung tied in a cloth restrains restless infants, especially girls. Gums smeared with goat's milk or the brain of a hare make for easy teething. Cato <note>Cato the Elder</note> thinks that sleep is induced by taking hare as food. The common people also believe it gives beauty to the body for nine days as a trivial matter <note>original: "fritolo loco," likely "frivolo loco"</note>. There must be some reason for such a strong belief. The Magi say that sleep is enticed by the bile of a sacrificed goat, provided it is smeared on the eyes or placed under the pillow. The ash of a goat's horn with myrtle oil stops sweats when rubbed on. Sexual intercourse is stimulated by applying wild boar's bile. Likewise swine marrow swallowed. Donkey fat mixed with the grease of a male goose and applied. Likewise, from the mating of a horse, Virgil...

<summary>This page catalogs various animal-based remedies for gynecological health, childbirth, and pediatric care, citing authorities like Olympias of Thebes and Cato. It includes treatments for infertility, labor complications, teething, and epilepsy using materials ranging from donkey milk to wolf teeth.</summary>
